title: Local bands, minstrels and the woman pianist
summary: He names the minstrel bands he heard, says he left Texarkana about 1912, and recalls playing Saturday dances with a hot woman pianist; boys shunned piano.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Do you remember any of the danced orchestras or bands around? What kind of music they played? What? How big the bands were? What kind of a band? What kind of music? If it was ragtime or waltzes or what kind of music they played?

Oh, well, I heard several of the bands. The best bands I heard before I went out on my own was the mysterious mistral bands, such as the Rabbit Foot, A.G. Allen Mistral, and, uh, The Dandy Dixie Mistral, The Georgia Mistral, The Algae Fields, The Blue Dock Stata. I heard it all about that.
Um, how late, uh, how long did you stay in Texarkana?
Oh, I stayed there until about 1912.
What was your first job? Did you play any music professionally? That is, did you get along to any band there before you left?
No, I used to play with the piano player, play dances.
You did play dances, though, before you left? Yeah. Excellent. Do you remember who the piano player was? What kind of music did you know?

I just can't, she was a woman, I just can't think of her name now, but she was the hottest piano player around town, and we played generally all the little dances, little Saturday night get-togethers. For 75 cents a dollar and a half, or anything like that.

Do you remember when you were a boy in New Orleans that some of the people say that the piano was considered sort of a sissy instrument and most of the boys wouldn't take up piano? Was that true in your hometown, do you think, the reason this girl, good pianist, the boys didn't take it up or not?
Well, that's right, the boys didn't go for the piano much. They wanted the horns, brass horns, playinets, and so forth.
